chapter_theme: The last fifteen stanzas of Agappei Siddhar close the work on the inner demon with a string of prohibitions: no sastra, no study or doing, no begging, no adornment, no sophistry, no agitation, no wanting even of moksha or initiation, no eating of the five, no joining in samadhi, no seeking in nadanta, no reciting the Veda, no claiming to have seen the truth, no trusting even the feet. Between them stand the few affirmations the poet allows: one must know oneself and join without joining, and everything else known is a ghoul's knowledge; where desire has ended, there is the Lord; the real is like salt in water; what appears is void, appearing without appearing in the pure space; and the world is mere coming and going, which, called true, yields release.
structure_note: 1717 to 1719 move from sastra and study to the one requirement, self-knowledge; 1720 to 1722 deal with the renunciant's outward signs (begging, adornment, show) and give the salt-in-water figure; 1723 to 1725 describe those who want nothing and deny that anyone has seen; 1726 to 1729 dismiss the yogic goals (samadhi, nadanta, union) and name the void and the pure space; 1730 and 1731 close with the coming and going of the world and a last set of prohibitions.

1717.reading: There is no sastra, demon; it has gone beyond motion; it must not be looked at, and it does not reach imagination.
1717.nuance: சலனம் கடந்தது, past all movement, is a description of the real; the sastras, which are movement of thought, do not touch it. பாவனை (imagining, visualising) is denied as a means here and in 1731.

1718.reading: What if you study, demon, and what if you do anything? All the ways that were told, you have seen, are what was pointed to (or, were burnt).
1718.nuance: The stanza dismisses study and action together. சுட்டது, as in 1679, is either 'pointed out' (the told ways are only pointers) or 'burnt' (they are consumed); the first reading makes the ways signs, the second makes them refuse.

1719.reading: You must know yourself, demon; you must join without joining; everything known after that is a ghoul's knowledge.
1719.nuance: The work's positive teaching in one stanza: self-knowledge, and union that is not attachment (சாராமற் சார). பேயறிவு (a ghoul's knowledge, with a pun on the demon addressed) is the Tirumanthiram's phrase for knowing that leaves out the self.

1720.reading: Even if you take to begging, demon, birth will not end; where desire has ceased, you have seen our Lord.
1720.nuance: பிச்சை, the mendicant's bowl, is set aside as 1691 set aside forest tapas: outward renunciation does not end birth. இச்சை அற்றவிடம் repeats 1683's desireless place, now with the Lord in it.

1721.reading: No adornment, demon, and no sophistry; no trickery, and no agitation.
1721.nuance: கோலம் (adornment, the ascetic's painted guise), குதர்க்கம் (perverse argument), சாலம் (deceit) and சஞ்சலம் (restlessness) are four faults in two lines, the outer show and the inner unrest of the false renunciant.

1722.reading: It is no pretence, demon, on your oath I have told you; like salt with water, inquire and remain.
1722.nuance: அப்புடன் உப்பு, salt in water, is a classic image of the real pervading the world without being seen apart from it; the stanza asks the demon to inquire and then stay (இருப்பாயே) in that dissolved state, the stillness of 1679 given a figure.

1723.reading: They want no moksha, demon, and want no release; they want no initiation, those who have become pure consciousness.
1723.nuance: சின்மயம் is the state of being knowledge itself, as the gloss says. The stanza denies to such people even the wish for release and for தீட்சை (the guru's initiation), completing 1665's 'join with nothing' and 1706's denial of release's ground.

1724.reading: The child is a ghost, demon; if you look, he is a madman; he is not the three times, and he is not an effect.
1724.nuance: பாலன் may be the Lord as the child (Murugan, or the infant Siva of the Siddhars' cipher), who seems a ghost or madman to ordinary sight, or the jnani whom the world calls mad, as Sivavakkiyar says of the siddhar. காலம் மூன்றுமல்ல and காரியம் அல்ல deny time and causation to him, so the Lord reading fits the second half.

1725.reading: What was seen is not, demon; if there were any who had seen, would they want what they had taken in? On your oath I have told you.
1725.nuance: The syntax is compressed: either no one has seen, since what is seen is not the real, or those who truly saw would no longer want (உண்டது வேண்டடியோ, would they want what was eaten?). Both readings deny that seeing and wanting can go together, as 1671 did.

1726.reading: Do not eat the five, demon, and do not want desire; let go of the heart too, and do not join in samadhi.
1726.nuance: அஞ்சு (the five) is the five senses' objects, or perhaps the five grains; 'eating' them is indulgence. நிட்டை, the yogic absorption the gloss calls Siva-yoga, is forbidden along with desire: even the yogi's goal is a joining, and the poet has said to join with nothing.

1727.reading: Do not seek in the truth of nadanta either, demon, I tell you; the alertness above it, do not believe to be true.
1727.nuance: நாதாந்தம், the end of nada, is one of the six ends (ஆறந்தம்) where the Tirumanthiram places high attainment; the stanza says not to seek even there. சூதானம் (glossed as alertness or caution) is obscure; the watchfulness of the yogi above nadanta seems meant, and it too is denied.

1728.reading: If one joins with another, demon, the one will perish, see; even the Parasiva that stands will not stand.
1728.nuance: ஒன்றோடு ஒன்று கூடில் may describe union with the Lord as the loss of the one who joins, so that even the standing Parasiva 'does not stand' as a separate object; or it may warn that any joining, any dualism of two things, destroys. On the first reading the stanza describes sayujya from the far side.

1729.reading: All the deeds that appear, demon, you have seen to be void; they appear without appearing, in the pure space.
1729.nuance: சூனியம், the void, is used of the appearing deeds (or appearances, தோன்றும் வினைகள்); சுத்த வெளி, the pure space, is where they appear without appearing. The stanza gives the work's ontology in one breath: what shows is empty, and the ground is open space, the Siddhars' பாழ்.

1730.reading: Do not say it is false, demon; it is only coming and going; when you call it true, release may be had.
1730.nuance: A correction to 1729: the world is not to be dismissed as பொய் but seen as போக்குவரத்து, traffic, mere passage. Calling that true, that is, seeing impermanence as the truth of appearances, is itself release; the stanza refuses both the realist and the illusionist poles.

1731.reading: Do not recite the Veda, demon; do not say 'we have seen the truth'; do not trust the feet; do not look by imagining.
1731.nuance: The last stanza turns the prohibitions on the poet's own supports: the guru's feet, named as the end in 1661, 1696 and 1705, are not to be trusted either, and the claim to have seen the truth (மெய்கண்டோம், the name of the Siddhanta's founding teacher) is forbidden. The work ends in the silence it began by asking for.

links.note: Tirumular says knowing oneself is knowledge and anything known afterwards is a ghoul's knowledge (பேயறிவு); Agappei repeats the line almost word for word, you must know yourself and all else known is பேயறிவு, with the pun that his addressee is the demon. The stanza is a direct borrowing of the Tirumanthiram's half-verse.

The Kural says that even with the fivefold awareness there is no benefit for those who lack true perception; Agappei asks what use study or doing is, since all the told ways are only pointers. Both deny that acquired knowledge avails without the inner seeing, though the Kural keeps learning and Agappei discards it.

The Kural says those called freed are those freed of craving and no others; Agappei says begging does not end birth and the Lord is where desire has ceased. Both put freedom in the ending of desire rather than in the outward act of renunciation, and both deny the title to the one who has only given up possessions.

Tirumular says the Siva-siddhas cast off the three graded releases as flawed, lose pride and change 'mine' and 'I'; Agappei says those who have become pure consciousness want no moksha, no release and no initiation. Tirumular rejects the lesser releases for the sake of union; Agappei's knowers want nothing at all, release included.

Sivavakkiyar says those who can melt sun, moon and stars into the one letter in the incomparable void (ஒப்பிலாத வெளி) and stay there are not born again; Agappei says appearances are void and appear without appearing in the pure space (சுத்த வெளி). Both name an open space beyond the lights of the inner sky as the ground of release.

Tirumular says that though one recites the Vedas and Agamas, what is ours lies in one letter of the Lord, to be mastered; Agappei says not to recite the Veda, not to trust the feet, and in 1707 not to open the mouth for mantra at all. The conflict holds if Tirumular's one letter is a mantra to be practised; it eases if the letter is read as the Lord himself.

new_concepts.gloss: the void: the Siddhars' name for the emptiness of all that appears, and for the open ground in which it appears, distinguished from பாழ் as the term the verses use for the appearances themselves rather than the residue left after maya is gone
new_concepts.label_source: the verse uses the word (1729 சூனியங் கண்டாயே)

source_issues: 1726 line 1 அஞ்சயும் is a misprint for அஞ்சையும்.
1731 line 2 மெய்கண்டோ ம் has a space inserted inside the word.
1727 line 3 சூதானம் is obscure; the gloss (சாக்கிரதை, alertness) is a guess at a word that may be corrupt.
